narrative_stages.label: Origin
narrative_stages.headline: Founded on a bet that EVs could be genuinely desirable
narrative_stages.detail: Tesla was founded in 2003 on the idea that electric cars didn't have to be slow, ugly compromises — they could be cars people actually wanted. Elon Musk joined a year later as an early investor and chairman before becoming CEO, and the company spent its first decade proving that idea one very expensive car at a time.

narrative_stages.label: Struggle
narrative_stages.headline: Near-bankruptcy and Model 3 "production hell"
narrative_stages.detail: Tesla nearly ran out of cash multiple times in its early years, and the 2017–2018 push to mass-produce the Model 3 became infamous as "production hell" — Musk slept at the factory as the company scrambled to avoid collapse. For years, skeptics openly bet against Tesla ever building cars at real volume, profitably.

narrative_stages.label: Inflection
narrative_stages.headline: First profitable year, S&P 500 inclusion, re-rated as a tech bet
narrative_stages.detail: Tesla posted its first full year of profitability, joined the S&P 500, and split its stock twice as investors began pricing it less like a car company and more like a technology platform with optionality in self-driving and energy storage. That reframing is a big part of why Tesla still trades at a premium most automakers never touch.

narrative_stages.label: Today
narrative_stages.headline: Growth reaccelerating, margins compressed, story now hinges on robotaxis
narrative_stages.detail: Revenue over the past year is $103.62 billion, and growth just reaccelerated to 25.5% in the latest quarter after a bumpy 2025. But net income fell 35% and gross margin compressed to about 17%, largely from price cuts against cheaper Chinese EVs. At a $1.44 trillion valuation — six times Toyota's, despite Toyota selling three times more — the market is really betting on robotaxis, humanoid robots, and energy storage, a bet the stock's own sharp swings show is still very much unresolved.

growth_playbook.stage_explainer: Companies in transition are pivoting their growth story from one core business to a new bet — investors have to decide whether to value the old business, the new one, or both, which is exactly why Tesla's stock swings so hard.
growth_playbook.lever_name: New Products & New Markets (robotaxi, humanoid robots, energy storage)
growth_playbook.lever_detail: Rather than squeezing more growth from car sales — where it's cutting prices just to hold volume — Tesla is betting its next growth chapter comes from autonomous ride-hailing, the Optimus robot, and grid-scale batteries.
growth_playbook.biggest_risk: The new bets could take years longer to generate real revenue than the market is currently pricing in, while the core car business keeps losing margin to cheaper competitors in the meantime.
growth_playbook.what_to_watch: Automotive gross margin specifically — if it keeps compressing while the new bets aren't yet generating meaningful revenue, that's the growth story cracking in real time.

reddit_pulse.summary_note: Illustrative example of common viewpoints in investor discussions about Tesla — curated for this demo rather than a live scrape, and opinion, not fact.

thought_bubbles.take: A common critique is that Tesla's valuation still assumes a future that hasn't arrived — with net income shrinking and margins compressed, the stock is seen by some as priced for robotaxis and robots, not the car business actually in front of investors today.

The bull case many people describe isn't about vehicle sales at all — it's the belief that autonomous driving and the Optimus humanoid robot program could eventually dwarf the auto business, making today's car-industry comparisons beside the point.

Early riders and testers of the robotaxi rollout often describe a mixed experience — genuinely impressive in places, but slowed by cautious routing and regulatory scrutiny, suggesting the commercial timeline may stretch longer than the most optimistic projections.

A recurring, less dramatic theme is simply competitive pressure: Chinese EV makers scaling fast and undercutting on price are treated as a real, ongoing constraint on Tesla's margins and global market share, independent of how the AI bets play out.
